pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: `Split` returns `(share, remainder int, err error)` — three values. Show how you would call it and say what each returned value means.
expected_points: one variable per result, in order: share, remainder, err := Split(...)
share and remainder are the normal results; err reports failure
every result must be assigned or explicitly discarded with _

questions.prompt: What is the (result, error) convention? What does a nil error mean, and what should a caller do before using the other results?
expected_points: a function that can fail returns its results plus a final error value
nil error means success; non-nil describes what went wrong
check if err != nil first — on failure the other results are just zero values

questions.prompt: What do named return values give you, and when do they hurt readability?
expected_points: the signature documents which result is which, e.g. two ints of the same type
the names are real variables starting at their zero values, and a bare return returns them (naked return)
naked returns hurt in longer functions — the reader must scan back to find what is returned; prefer explicit return values

questions.prompt: What does `prices ...int` in a signature mean? You have `nums := []int{1, 2, 3}` — how do you pass it to `Sum`, and why doesn't `Sum(nums)` compile?
expected_points: the function accepts any number of int arguments; inside, prices is a []int slice
spread it at the call site: Sum(nums...)
Sum(nums) fails because nums is a []int where int arguments are expected

questions.prompt: `SplitBill` could loop over the prices and do the division itself. Why is building it from `Sum` and `Split` better?
expected_points: each function keeps one responsibility, so failures and changes are localized
Sum and Split are already tested; SplitBill only connects them
the guard (people < 1) lives in exactly one place instead of being duplicated

questions.prompt: You only need the share from `Split`. How do you discard the remainder — and would you ever discard the error the same way?
expected_points: use the blank identifier: share, _, err := Split(...)
discarding the error hides failure — almost always wrong; check it instead
the compiler forces you to make ignoring a result visible and deliberate
